name: Rome
title: An arena. A ruin. A city that kept going.
deck: The Colosseum survived as its surroundings and purpose changed. Read the city as layers, rather than a single ancient moment.
archiveType: Photochrom print · historical colours added in printing
modernTitle: The Colosseum in the present-day city
changed: From an imperial spectacle to an archaeological landmark: the structure remains, but the way people use and understand it has changed.
persisted: The amphitheatre still anchors how visitors recognise Rome. Survival, adaptation, excavation, and conservation all belong to its history.
notice: Look at the exposed interior in the archive print. A familiar monument was already a ruin long before today’s visitor experience.
eras: The amphitheatre belonged to a much wider city of forums, public monuments, infrastructure, and imperial power.
Another city within the old one
Religious and public buildings added new centres of activity alongside the remains of antiquity. Rome did not stop developing when imperial rule changed.
The archive print presents an already ancient monument to an expanding audience for travel images. It documents its own era, not the arena in Roman times.
A living city around an archaeological site
The Colosseum is both a protected monument and part of modern Rome. Its meaning now includes research, conservation, and public access.

name: Istanbul
title: The water stayed. The capital changed.
deck: Read a city shaped by different empires through its enduring maritime setting and its changing skyline.
archiveTitle: The Golden Horn, then called Constantinople
archiveType: Photochrom print · historical colours added in printing
modernTitle: Galata Bridge across the Golden Horn
changed: Different political and religious centres added new buildings to the skyline. The historic city now sits inside a much larger metropolis.
persisted: The water remains a powerful organising feature. The Golden Horn and Bosphorus still help explain how districts face and connect with one another.
notice: Notice how densely the historic waterfront was already built. The archive is a late Ottoman-era view, not an image of Byzantine Constantinople.
eras: Hagia Sophia became one of the city’s defining monumental buildings, reflecting its role as a major religious and political centre.
Buildings including the Süleymaniye Mosque added another architectural layer. Later power did not erase every trace of earlier urban life.
The historical view records the Golden Horn in the late Ottoman period. The name Constantinople in its catalogue belongs to that archival record.
Historic waterfronts and monuments remain within a growing urban region. The challenge is caring for these layers while everyday city life continues.

name: London
title: One river. Many generations of crossings.
deck: London Bridge offers a thread through a city repeatedly rebuilt around the Thames.
archiveTitle: London Bridge in a late-Victorian print
archiveType: Photochrom print · historical colours added in printing
modernTitle: A present-day view of London Bridge
changed: The bridge in the historical print is not the bridge standing here now. Structures, traffic, and the skyline change even when a crossing keeps its name.
persisted: The Thames crossing remains a useful connection between the banks. A long-lived route need not depend on one long-lived structure.
notice: Compare the bridge forms and their surroundings. These are different bridges and viewpoints, not a perfectly aligned before-and-after pair.

sources.name: UK Parliament · Rebuilding after the Great Fire

eras: A crossing helps make a town
Londinium developed with a bridge, roads, and river trade. The crossing connected movement on land with activity along the Thames.
The Great Fire destroyed much of the City. A rebuilding act followed in 1667, shaping how the damaged city was reconstructed.
This print shows an earlier London Bridge and a working river landscape. Its date matters: it does not depict the medieval bridge or the modern one.
Today’s London Bridge continues a long history of crossing at this part of the Thames, within a markedly changed cityscape.

name: Cairo
title: A city grew beyond its first boundaries.
deck: An archive view from the Nile opens a longer story: a medieval capital became one layer within a much larger urban landscape.
archiveType: Historical photochrom view · colour is a printing treatment
modernTitle: A wider view of present-day Cairo
changed: The modern urban landscape extends around older districts and monuments. The archive riverbank view is one fragment of that longer expansion.
persisted: Riverfront activity and long-established neighbourhoods remain part of Cairo’s story. The medieval city is still legible within later urban layers.
notice: The old view documents a working Nile shore. It is not a photograph of medieval Cairo, and it does not show the whole nineteenth-century city.

sources.name: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities · Historical Cairo

eras: The Fatimids founded al-Qahira northeast of earlier settlements. Al-Azhar was commissioned soon afterwards, giving the new city a major institution.
Mosques, schools, fountains, and other buildings contributed to a major urban and cultural centre. Historic Cairo preserves many layers rather than one frozen date.
The archive image shows the Nile shore near Bulaq, including a sailing vessel. It is evidence of a particular riverside scene in a later era.
A historic city inside a metropolis
Older neighbourhoods and monumental buildings coexist with much later growth. A photograph of one district cannot stand for the entire city.

name: Kyoto
title: A capital moved. A cultural city endured.
deck: Kyoto’s story continues after its imperial role changed. Streets, wooden buildings, and cultural practices carry different kinds of continuity.
archiveType: Hand-coloured albumen photograph · unknown photographer, Rijksmuseum collection
modernTitle: A present-day street in Gion, Kyoto
changed: The political centre shifted, while later infrastructure and modern urban life altered the city. Historic wooden streets survive through continued care, not by being untouched.
persisted: Kyoto retained a strong cultural identity after its imperial role ended. Building traditions and gardens remain important alongside everyday urban change.
notice: Look at the decorated street in the historical photograph. The modern view is another Kyoto street, not a claim that this exact scene survives unchanged.

sources.name: UNESCO · Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
Kyoto official tourism · History of Kyoto

eras: Heian-kyo was established as a new capital, drawing on Chinese capital planning. It became the setting for a long development of Japanese culture.
Kyoto’s role changed as the imperial centre moved to Tokyo. Losing that political role did not mean losing the city’s cultural life.
This archival photograph documents street decorations. Its hand colouring is part of the historical object, not evidence that the camera captured colour naturally.
Traditional streets, wooden architecture, and gardens exist alongside a modern city. Preservation is an ongoing choice involving buildings and the people who use them.
